h1: Choosing an SEO agency for Dubai and the wider UAE
metaTitle: Which Is the Best SEO Agency in Dubai?
metaDescription: What UAE search really needs: Arabic and English dual intent, .ae signals, local citations, and the AED-versus-INR maths behind hiring an offshore team.
answer: No agency is best for every Dubai business. The real decision is local versus offshore: UAE agencies commonly quote AED 4,000–15,000 a month, Indian teams a fraction of that in INR. Pay the local premium when your demand is Arabic-language, licence-gated or relationship-led. Otherwise offshore handles content and technical work fine.
takeaways: Dubai is a **two-language market**, and the two behave differently. English carries most B2B and expat commercial search; Arabic carries government-adjacent, legal, healthcare and community demand.
Machine-translating your English site into Arabic and adding hreflang is the most expensive mistake in UAE SEO.
The offshore case is stronger in Dubai than almost anywhere: **90 minutes of time difference** and a matching Monday–Friday week.
The dirham is pegged to the US dollar, so the AED–INR rate moves with the rupee. Convert at today's rate before you compare quotes.

sections.h2: Dubai searches in two languages, and they don't behave the same
body: The UAE population is overwhelmingly expatriate, and English is the working language of most commerce. That pushes a lot of high-value B2B search — logistics, free zone setup, enterprise software, professional services — almost entirely into English.

Arabic isn't a smaller version of the same demand. It concentrates where language and identity matter: government-adjacent services, legal and family matters, healthcare, education, religious and community topics, and a good deal of consumer research among Emirati and wider Arab audiences. Nobody publishes a reliable split, so don't let an agency quote one at you — pull your own Search Console query data by country and language before deciding what to fund.
The mechanics of Arabic SEO are genuinely different work, not a translation task.
bullets: **Right-to-left layout** breaks templates that were never tested for it — navigation, forms, breadcrumbs, mixed-direction numerals.
**Modern Standard Arabic versus Gulf dialect.** People write formal Arabic and search in something closer to how they speak. Keyword lists built from MSA alone miss real demand.
**Diacritics and spelling variance.** Searchers type without diacritics and with several accepted spellings of the same word, which fragments volume across variants your tool may report separately.
**Weaker tool coverage.** Arabic keyword volumes in Western tools are thinner and less reliable than English. Search Console and on-the-ground input matter more than usual.
**Transliteration.** Brand and place names appear in both scripts, and you need both to show up for either.

callout.title: The mistake that costs the most
callout.body: Running your English pages through machine translation, publishing them at `/ar/` and wiring hreflang to them. You get a full Arabic site that reads as machine output to every Arabic speaker who lands on it, and you've now got twice the pages to maintain. Translate fewer pages, properly, with a native writer.

sections.h2: The .ae question and the signals that actually place you in the UAE
body: Domain choice is where UAE conversations usually start and it's rarely the biggest lever. A ccTLD is a strong geographic signal, but it also confines you — if you sell into Saudi and Qatar too, a `.com` with proper hreflang is usually the better structure.

Registration rules matter more than ranking theory here. `.com.ae` has historically required UAE trade licence documentation, so check current requirements with an accredited registrar before you build a plan around it. If you're a free zone entity, confirm which of your licence documents the registrar accepts.
The signals that reliably tell Google you serve the UAE are less glamorous.
numbered: A **Google Business Profile** with a genuine UAE address, correct category and photos that aren't stock. In Dubai, include the Makani number in your address details — it's the addressing system people and couriers actually use.
**Consistent NAP** — name, address, phone — across every listing, with a +971 number that a human answers.
**Prices in AED** on the page, plus VAT treatment stated. UAE VAT is 5%, and buyers notice when a site quotes in dollars.
**hreflang** set to `en-AE` and `ar-AE` if you run both languages, with a sensible `x-default`. Get this wrong and you'll cannibalise yourself across markets.
**Links from UAE domains** — chambers, associations, regional press, partners. This is the hardest signal to fake and the one most offshore teams under-deliver on.

callout.title: Hosting is not the lever
callout.body: Where your server sits is close to irrelevant for UAE ranking, and any agency that leads with "we'll move you to a Dubai server" is selling a 2012 checklist. Latency matters for Core Web Vitals; a CDN solves that without moving anything.

sections.h2: Citations and directories that actually exist in the UAE
body: Local citation lists written for the US are useless here. Yelp is irrelevant, and half the aggregators an agency will submit you to have no UAE presence at all. The platforms that matter in the Emirates are a different set, and several of them are vertical rather than general.

Prioritise by whether real buyers use the platform to choose, not by whether it passes a link. Property searches in the UAE run through Bayut and Property Finder. Food ordering runs through Talabat, Deliveroo and Zomato. Classifieds and used goods run through Dubizzle. If you're in one of those categories, your listing there is worth more than fifty generic citations.

For general business presence, work through your Google Business Profile first, then chamber of commerce and free-zone member directories, then established UAE business directories and regional press listings. Expat community forums and neighbourhood groups drive real referral traffic even when the links are nofollowed.

sections.h2: AED rates versus INR rates — the arithmetic
body: There's no published benchmark for UAE agency retainers, so treat the band below as the range of quotes you'll encounter rather than a survey figure. Dubai agency pricing carries genuine local costs — office rent, licensing, visa sponsorship, salaries indexed to a high cost of living — and those costs are real regardless of the quality of the work they fund.
The question isn't which number is smaller. It's which parts of the work actually require someone inside the UAE.

callout.title: Check the currency before the quote
callout.body: The dirham is pegged to the US dollar, so AED–INR moves entirely with the rupee. A twelve-month budget built on one snapshot of the rate is a bet on the rupee you didn't mean to place. Agree the contract currency explicitly, and agree who absorbs movement.

sections.h2: Timezone: the strongest offshore argument in the region
body: India is 90 minutes ahead of the UAE. That's it. A 10am call in Dubai is 11:30am in Bangalore, and a Dubai team leaving at 6pm overlaps almost the entire Indian working day.

The working week lines up too. The UAE shifted to a Monday-to-Friday week in 2022, which removed the old Friday–Saturday weekend mismatch that used to cost offshore engagements a day a week in dropped handoffs.

Compare that with the same decision in Australia or the UK, where you're negotiating over a two-hour window or an eight-hour gap. In the Gulf, offshore delivery works with no process gymnastics at all — which is why so much of the region's agency work is already produced in India, sometimes by the local agency you're quoting.

callout.title: Worth asking your Dubai shortlist
callout.body: "Which parts of this are produced in-house in the UAE, and which are subcontracted?" It's a fair question, the answer is often "content and links are produced offshore", and it reframes the entire price comparison.

sections.h2: When to hire locally, and where we'd fit
body: Hire a UAE agency when your growth depends on Arabic-first content, on regional PR relationships, on tender and government-adjacent work, or on a physical retail footprint where someone needs to visit branches and collect reviews in person. Those are real reasons and worth the premium.

Hire offshore when the constraint is capacity: technical work, English content at volume, structured data, migrations, reporting, and the slow compounding work that eats hours rather than relationships.

Our SEO retainers start at ₹75,000/mo, with smaller sites from ₹40,000/mo, ex-GST, month-to-month after the first quarter, and you keep every asset. We don't claim to run Arabic digital PR from Bangalore — when a client needs it, it gets sourced locally and priced honestly. One thing doesn't change with the currency: we guarantee movement against your own frozen 90-day baseline of qualified organic leads, never a ranking position. Miss it in 90 days and we keep working free until we beat it.

faqs.q: How much does SEO cost in Dubai?
faqs.a: UAE agencies commonly quote between AED 4,000 and AED 15,000 a month, with enterprise programmes above that. There's no published benchmark, so treat those as observed quote ranges. Offshore Indian teams typically price well below that band — ours start at ₹75,000/mo — because the cost base is different, not the work.

faqs.q: Do I need an Arabic version of my website for UAE SEO?
faqs.a: Only if your buyers search in Arabic. Pull your Search Console query data by country and language first. If Arabic demand is real, translate a small set of pages properly with a native Gulf-Arabic writer rather than machine-translating the whole site — a bad Arabic version damages trust faster than having none.

faqs.q: Is a .ae domain necessary to rank in the UAE?
faqs.a: No. A ccTLD is a strong geographic signal but it confines you to one market, which is a problem if you also sell into Saudi or Qatar. A .com with correct hreflang, a UAE Google Business Profile and UAE links performs fine. Check registrar requirements before planning around .com.ae.

faqs.q: Can an Indian SEO agency work for a Dubai business?
faqs.a: Yes, and the timezone makes it unusually practical — India is 90 minutes ahead of the UAE and both run a Monday-to-Friday week. Technical work, English content, analytics and reporting travel well. Arabic writing and UAE digital PR need local people whether your agency is local or not.

faqs.q: Which local directories matter for SEO in the UAE?
faqs.a: Start with Google Business Profile, then chamber of commerce and free-zone member directories and established UAE business listings. Vertical platforms usually matter more than general ones: Bayut and Property Finder for property, Talabat and Deliveroo for food, Dubizzle for classifieds. US citation checklists are close to useless here.
